svg.title: Private VLAN: one primary VLAN split into isolated and community segments behind a promiscuous port, and why it lost to SGT and VXLAN
svg.desc: Top left: the three port roles inside one primary VLAN. The promiscuous port faces the gateway or load balancer and can talk to everything. Isolated ports on their own isolated secondary VLAN can talk only to the promiscuous port, not to each other. Community ports on the same community secondary VLAN can talk to each other and to the promiscuous port. Top right: the resulting communication matrix - isolated to isolated is blocked, isolated to community is blocked, community to community within the same community VLAN is allowed, and promiscuous to anything is allowed. Middle: where it fits - hotels, dormitories and apartments where every room is isolated but one subnet and one gateway are shared; several web servers in a DMZ where a compromised server must not reach its peers; and carrier access where customer isolation is the product. Bottom: four reasons it stayed niche - configuration complexity with vendor differences, difficulty across switches because VTPv3 or manual synchronisation drifts, no equivalent inside VXLAN/EVPN overlays, and troubleshooting where a failure could be PVLAN, an ACL or routing and nothing says which. The modern replacements are SGT with policy in the campus and VXLAN with micro-segmentation in the data centre.
svg.text: Private VLAN: split one subnet into segments the switch enforces, without touching the gateway
Everyone keeps the same address range and the same default gateway, but peers simply cannot reach each other
ONE PRIMARY VLAN · THREE PORT ROLES
primary VLAN 100 - one subnet, one SVI, one gateway
Secondary VLANs do not get an SVI. The gateway lives only on the primary VLAN,
which is why the subnet does not change when you turn PVLAN on.
Isolated ports: gateway only. Community ports: each other plus gateway. Promiscuous: everything.
No ACL, no extra subnet, no routing change.
The decision is made by the port's own role.
Every room isolated, one shared subnet and gateway -
resident-to-resident traffic never happens by design
Several web servers in a DMZ
isolated ports plus one promiscuous load balancer: a compromised server cannot
1 · Complex, and vendors differ in behaviour
2 · Hard across switches - VTPv3 or hand sync that drifts
4 · Ambiguous to troubleshoot: PVLAN, ACL or route?
Replacements: SGT + policy in the campus, VXLAN + EPG in the DC
PVLAN buys port isolation at the price of a construct nobody else in the network understands. In a greenfield design the same
outcome usually comes cheaper from a segmentation tag (SGT) or from simply cutting a second VLAN - and both survive the move to an overlay.
Rule of thumb: if the requirement is "same subnet, no peer traffic, old hardware", PVLAN is the only tool. In every other case it is the wrong tool.
